b: Death of fat cells in the breast, usually following trauma or surgery. Dead fat cells trigger an inflammatory reaction that heals by scarring — and that scar can look and feel exactly like cancer.
About half of patients have a history of breast trauma or prior surgery
The other half have no obvious cause
Fat cells are injured → central liquefactive necrosis forms

snip.t: Pancreatic injury → premature enzyme activation and inflammatory mediator release → pancreatic oedema and inflammation → possible fat necrosis and tissue necrosis → systemic inflammatory response → possible organ dysfunction.
The enzymes released from the pancreas with acute pancreatitis damage the surrounding fat and form soaps -- localized soft tan to yellow areas of fat necrosis.
Extravasation of the milk may produce chronic inflammation and even fat necrosis.
Once the pancreatitis has started, the formation of the chalky soap deposits of fat necrosis may draw off calcium to produce hypocalcemia.
| Fat Necrosis | History of trauma/surgery (~50%); mimics cancer; liquefactive necrosis → giant cells/calcification → scarring |

qs.q: During an exploratory laparotomy, a surgeon notes pancreatic inflammation and peripancreatic fat necrosis. Which specific anatomical component makes up the vast majority (85 to 90%) of the healthy human pancreas?
o: Specialised ductal epithelial cells lining the main pancreatic tree
Endocrine islets of Langerhans producing crucial regulatory hormones
Peripancreatic fat lobules surrounding the entire retroperitoneal organ
Exocrine acinar cells responsible for digestive enzyme production
qs.e: The exocrine pancreas, composed of acinar cells, makes up 85 to 90% of the organ and secretes digestive enzymes. The endocrine islets represent a much smaller fraction of the pancreatic mass.
qs.s: Acute and Chronic Pancreatitis: Causes, Diagnosis, Severity Scoring: MCQs

qs.q: What is the primary reason why breast conditions such as duct ectasia and fat necrosis present a major clinical challenge?
o: They rapidly progress to systemic sepsis if not treated with aggressive antibiotics
They invariably transform into high-grade invasive ductal carcinomas over time
They cause extensive lymphatic obstruction leading to peau d'orange appearance
They frequently mimic breast carcinoma by causing hard masses and skin retraction
qs.e: Many benign inflammatory and degenerative breast conditions clinically and radiologically mimic invasive breast cancer by producing hard masses, calcifications, and retraction. They do not transform into cancer or cause sepsis, but they must be carefully distinguished from malignancy.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: Which macroscopic and microscopic features are characteristic of long-standing fat necrosis in the breast?
o: Ill-defined firm gray-white nodules with small chalky-white calcified foci
Diffuse cystic spaces filled with purulent exudate and pasty white secretions
Hyperplastic lobules surrounded by dense cuffs of mature B-lymphocytes
Dilated subareolar ducts lined by keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium
qs.e: Later stages of fat necrosis form an ill-defined firm gray-white nodule containing small chalky-white calcified foci as the lesion heals by scarring. Purulent exudate and squamous metaplasia are features of acute mastitis and periductal mastitis respectively.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: What is the origin of the hemosiderin deposits found during the microscopic evolution of fat necrosis?
o: Breakdown of extravasated blood following initial cellular injury and hemorrhage.
Phagocytosis of exogenous foreign material introduced during breast surgery.
Metabolic breakdown of cholesterol crystals shed from ruptured duct walls.
Degradation of inspissated proteinaceous secretions within obstructed ducts.
qs.e: Hemosiderin deposits in fat necrosis arise from the breakdown of blood (hemorrhage) that occurs when fat cells are injured. Hemosiderin represents stored iron derived from degraded hemoglobin.
qs.s: Breast Inflammation: Mastitis, Periductal Mastitis & Duct Ectasia: MCQs

qs.q: A patient develops acute pancreatitis. Areas of fat necrosis in the peritoneum appear as chalky-white deposits. This appearance is due to:
o: Deposition of fibrin from vascular injury
Accumulation of cholesterol crystals
Formation of calcium soaps (saponification)
Infiltration by neutrophils with myeloperoxidase
qs.e: In fat necrosis, pancreatic lipases break down triglycerides to fatty acids, which combine with calcium to form calcium soaps—visible as chalky-white areas. This is saponification. This type of necrosis is specific to enzymatic fat breakdown, distinguishing it from other forms.
qs.s: Pathology MCQs: Cell Injury, Cell Death, and Adaptations

qs.q: Fat necrosis of the breast is clinically important primarily because
o: It indicates underlying BRCA1 mutation in young women
It causes bilateral nipple discharge requiring surgery
It frequently progresses to invasive lobular carcinoma
It can mimic carcinoma clinically and on mammography
qs.e: Fat necrosis produces a firm, sometimes calcified mass that can closely mimic carcinoma on examination and imaging. Biopsy is required to exclude malignancy.

o: Heart infarction
Lung infarction
Acute pancreatitis
Brain infarction
qs.e: Fat necrosis occurs when pancreatic enzymes (lipases) are released into the peritoneum in acute pancreatitis, breaking down fat cells. It also occurs in traumatic injury to adipose tissue such as breast tissue.

es.q: A patient develops hypocalcemia (Chvostek and Trousseau signs) during an episode of acute pancreatitis. What is the underlying mechanism for this electrolyte disturbance? → **Calcium is consumed by saponification (calcium binding with free fatty acids) during fat necrosis.**
es.m: - **Exocrine Failure**: **Exocrine pancreatic failure** has occurred, leading to the clinical presentation of steatorrhea and malabsorption.
es.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review — Essay Questions

es.q: A patient develops hypocalcemia (Chvostek and Trousseau signs) during an episode of acute pancreatitis. What is the underlying mechanism for this electrolyte disturbance? → Calcium is consumed by saponification (calcium binding with free fatty acids) during fat necrosis.
es.m:
- **Electrolyte disturbance**: Hypocalcemia during acute necrotizing pancreatitis.
- **Pathophysiological mechanism**: Release of pancreatic lipase into pancreatic tissue and retroperitoneum.
- **Fat necrosis**: Lipase breaks down triglycerides into free fatty acids.
- **Saponification**: Free fatty acids bind with serum calcium ions, forming insoluble calcium soaps.
- **Clinical consequence**: Depletion of circulating calcium leading to hypocalcemia and tetany.
es.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review — Essay Questions

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Fat necrosis is a benign, inflammatory reaction to injured adipose tissue, most often in the breast after trauma or surgery. It produces a firm, sometimes calcified mass that can mimic carcinoma on exam and imaging.

sections.p: Fat necrosis is death of adipocytes with subsequent saponification of released fatty acids and a granulomatous healing response. Diagnosis relies on clinical history, imaging (calcifications on mammogram) and, when uncertain, core biopsy showing necrotic fat, foamy macrophages and fibrosis.
b: Benign histology distinguishes it from carcinoma
Calcifications are often coarse and rim‑like

t.b: Does the lesion have coarse, rim‑like calcifications? → Typical of fat necrosis; spiculated microcalcifications suggest cancer.
Is there necrotic adipocytes with giant cells and fibrosis? → Confirms fat necrosis; presence of atypical cells warrants further work‑up.

sections.p: There is no formal staging system; severity is gauged by extent of necrosis and fibrosis. Small, self‑limited lesions heal with minimal scarring, whereas extensive necrosis can produce large, firm masses that may require excision.
b: Severe: >5 cm, persistent mass or ulceration

sections.p: The most common trigger is blunt trauma or surgical manipulation of the breast. In low‑resource settings, additional contributors include infection (e.g., mastitis), chronic inflammation from milk extravasation, and rarely, systemic conditions that cause fat breakdown.
b: Herbal poultices causing local fat irritation

sections.p: Patients notice a painless, firm lump that may feel irregular. Over weeks it can become firm, sometimes with overlying skin dimpling or retraction. Mammography may reveal coarse calcifications; ultrasound shows a hypoechoic mass with posterior shadowing.
Imaging and tissue sampling are used to differentiate fat necrosis from malignancy. When imaging is unavailable, clinical follow‑up and fine‑needle aspiration can guide management.

t.b: Is the lesion hypoechoic with posterior shadowing? → Supports fat necrosis; solid, irregular mass raises cancer suspicion.
Does the aspirate contain oily fluid and macrophages? → Suggests fat necrosis; cellular atypia prompts biopsy.
Can the lesion be monitored for change over 4–6 weeks? → Stability favors benign process; growth mandates biopsy.

sections.p: Although benign, fat necrosis can obscure cancer detection and, if large, cause skin ulceration or infection. Persistent growth, new skin changes, or systemic signs (fever, weight loss) require urgent reassessment.

Treat the underlying cause (e.g., control mastitis with antibiotics). Most lesions are observed; surgical excision is reserved for persistent, enlarging, or cosmetically concerning masses. Analgesics for pain and reassurance are essential.
b: Antibiotics (e.g., penicillin class) for concurrent infection
Surgical excision if lesion >5 cm, growing, or patient desires removal

sections.p: Re‑examine the breast clinically and with imaging at 3–6 months to ensure stability. Educate patients on avoiding breast trauma and promptly treating mastitis.
b: Repeat mammogram if initial imaging was equivocal
Avoid tight clothing or blunt injury to the breast

sections.p: Conditions that present as a firm breast mass with calcifications can be mistaken for fat necrosis.

Calcifications on mammography are not specific; coarse, rim‑like patterns favor fat necrosis, but fine, pleomorphic microcalcifications are typical of cancer. Biopsy sampling error can miss focal malignancy within a necrotic area.
b: Coarse calcifications may still coexist with cancer
Negative biopsy does not rule out cancer if sampling was limited

whenToSeekHelp: Fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss

faq.a: No, fat necrosis itself is benign, but it can mask an underlying carcinoma, so persistent or suspicious lesions need evaluation.

faq.q: Why does fat necrosis cause calcifications?
faq.a: Released fatty acids bind calcium, forming insoluble soaps that appear as coarse calcifications on imaging.
No, most cases resolve or remain stable with observation; surgery is reserved for large, symptomatic, or uncertain lesions.
